hypothesis: The KEGG ortholog K06159 (multidrug/microcin transport system ATP-binding/permease protein, an ABC-transporter component) is increased/characteristic in the gut metagenome of 5-month-old infants relative to 12-month-old infants.
rationale: No primary study was found that reports K06159 by ID (or its named homolog YbhF/YbhFSR-type multidrug/microcin ABC exporter) as differentially abundant between 5- and 12-month-old infants. However, several independent lines of indirect evidence point in the hypothesized direction: (i) a prospective metagenomic infant cohort (mSystems 2025) reported a significant decreasing trend with age in the abundance of 'ABC transporter' functional capacity in early infancy; (ii) PICRUSt-based analysis of milk- vs solid-fed infants found environmental information processing / membrane transport pathways over-represented in exclusively breastfed (i.e. developmentally earlier, pre-weaning) infants, whereas introduction of solids shifted hundreds of gene categories; (iii) the dominant taxonomic carriers of multidrug/microcin ABC exporter orthologs - Enterobacteriaceae/Escherichia - fall sharply in relative abundance between ~6 and 12 months in multiple independent infant cohorts, and infant-gut efflux/ABC-transporter resistome content declines over the first year in parallel with Proteobacteria dynamics. A bioRxiv preprint of a US infant randomized feeding trial comparing 5- vs 12-month timepoints also reported enrichment of 'transporter proteins' and E. coli biofilm genes in the 5-month group, but this source may describe the same cohort/data as the present study and is therefore treated as non-independent corroboration only. Because all support is pathway-, taxon- or preprint-level rather than a direct primary report of this specific KO in this specific contrast, this meets the 'multiple indirect studies pointing the same direction' criterion (score 2) rather than 3.
mechanism: K06159 corresponds to the ATP-binding/permease components of multidrug/microcin ABC export systems (e.g. the E. coli YbhFSR-type exporter, experimentally shown to efflux tetracyclines and cations, and related microcin secretion transporters), which are largely encoded by Proteobacteria/Enterobacteriaceae and other facultative anaerobes. At ~5 months the milk-dominated, low-diversity infant gut is comparatively rich in Enterobacteriaceae (E. coli, Klebsiella) and other early colonizers with high per-genome densities of ABC transport/efflux genes, and bacteriocin/microcin-mediated interbacterial antagonism is an important competitive strategy in this sparsely occupied niche. With complementary feeding by 12 months, obligate anaerobe Firmicutes/Bacteroidetes expand and Enterobacteriaceae contract, so the relative gene-level contribution of multidrug/microcin exporter orthologs is diluted while carbohydrate-degradation and fermentation functions rise - yielding higher relative abundance of K06159-type transporter genes at the earlier timepoint.

evidence.title: Gut microbiota development, antibiotic resistome, and related perinatal factors in early infancy
evidence.study_population: Prospective cohort of human infants, longitudinal fecal metagenomes in early infancy (first 6 months)
evidence.relevance: Reports a statistically significant decreasing trend with infant age in the abundance of ABC transporter functional capacity - the functional category to which K06159 belongs - supporting higher relative abundance at earlier ages.

evidence.title: Milk- and solid-feeding practices and daycare attendance are associated with differences in bacterial diversity, predominant communities, and metabolic and immune function of the infant gut microbiome
evidence.study_population: Human infants stratified by exclusive breastfeeding vs. non-exclusive breastfeeding with/without solid foods (pre- vs post-complementary feeding)
evidence.relevance: Exclusively breastfed (pre-weaning, developmentally analogous to the 5-month group) infants showed over-representation of environmental information processing / membrane transport pathways, the KEGG category containing ABC transporters such as K06159.

evidence.title: Stepwise establishment of functional microbial groups in the infant gut between 6 months and 2 years: A prospective cohort study
evidence.study_population: Prospective cohort of human infants sampled from 6 to 24 months
evidence.relevance: Shows Escherichia coli/Klebsiella/Shigella declining from 6 to 12 months; these Enterobacteriaceae are the principal carriers of multidrug/microcin ABC exporter genes, indirectly predicting higher K06159 relative abundance at the earlier timepoint.

evidence.title: Age-associated gut microbiome succession, colonization resistance, and relative resistome patterns in an antibiotic-restricted infant cohort
evidence.study_population: Antibiotic-restricted human infant cohort, age-stratified fecal microbiome/resistome
evidence.relevance: Documents a large decrease in Enterobacteriaceae relative abundance with age across the first year, the taxonomic substrate for enterobacterial multidrug/microcin ABC transport systems.

evidence.title: Antibiotic resistance gene dynamics in the commensal infant gut microbiome over the first year of life
evidence.study_population: Longitudinal human infant cohort, metagenomes over the first year of life
evidence.relevance: Finds a core infant resistome dominated by efflux/transport systems typical of Enterobacteriaceae, with overall gene carriage declining over the first year in step with Proteobacteria - consistent with higher multidrug-transporter gene abundance at 5 vs 12 months.

evidence.title: A Putative Efflux Transporter of the ABC Family, YbhFSR, in Escherichia coli Functions in Tetracycline Efflux and Na+(Li+)/H+ Transport
evidence.study_population: Escherichia coli laboratory strains (in vitro genetic/biochemical characterization)
evidence.relevance: Establishes the identity and function of the enterobacterial multidrug ABC exporter corresponding to this KO family, supporting the mechanistic link between K06159 abundance and Enterobacteriaceae/E. coli load in the infant gut.

evidence.title: Network-based representation learning reveals the impact of age and diet on the gut microbial and metabolomic environment of U.S. infants in a randomized controlled feeding trial
evidence.study_population: US infants in a randomized controlled complementary feeding trial (meat vs dairy protein), paired samples at 5 and 12 months
evidence.relevance: Directly compares 5- vs 12-month infant metagenomes and reports enrichment of transporter-protein genes, inorganic ion transport and E. coli biofilm genes in the 5-month group; however this likely describes the same cohort as the present study, so it is corroborative rather than independent.

contradicting_evidence: Evidence is not uniform: a metagenomic study of the complementary feeding transition (PLOS One, 4/9/12-month sampling) concluded that microbiome composition changed markedly while overall functional (KEGG) capacity remained comparatively stable, which argues against a strong age effect on generic transporter orthologs. Cross-sectional pediatric work also shows increasing gene richness and generally higher predicted transporter/ABC-transporter content in older/perturbed states, and the mSystems age trend was demonstrated within the first 6 months rather than across a 5- vs 12-month contrast. No study, however, reported K06159 (or a named homolog) as specifically higher at 12 months than at 5 months.

caveats: K06159 is a broadly distributed, functionally ambiguous ABC-transporter KO (annotated as 'multidrug/microcin' export) present across many bacterial genera, so its metagenomic abundance is a composite signal strongly influenced by taxonomic turnover rather than a specific biological process; no published study quantifies this exact KO in a 5- vs 12-month infant comparison. Pathway-level ('ABC transporters', 'membrane transport') findings can behave differently from individual KOs, and PICRUSt-predicted functions add inference error. The one source that directly matches the 5- vs 12-month contrast is a preprint that plausibly reports the same cohort as this study, so it cannot be counted as independent external validation; relative-abundance (compositional) effects also mean an apparent 5-month enrichment may reflect dilution by expanding fiber-degrading taxa at 12 months rather than absolute gene increase.
